503: 
504: ### Section 2: SMART ROUTING (Required for All Skills)
505: 
506: **Purpose**: Use this section to explain how you route a request to this skill's resources.
507: 
508: **Three skill kinds, one shape**:
509: 
510: | Kind | How to tell | What Section 2 says |
511: |------|-------------|---------------------|
512: | Hub | the folder holds `mode-registry.json` and `hub-router.json` | how a prompt reaches a mode, and where the root `ROUTER.md` is |
513: | Mode packet | a packet folder inside a hub | what selects this packet, what it loads first, and where its own `ROUTER.md` is |
514: | Standalone | neither hub file | the same as a mode packet, with the router in its own `ROUTER.md` |
515: 
516: **The limit**: 12 non-blank lines and 180 words are the hard ceilings the check enforces. Aim for 8 to 12 lines. A packet or standalone skill says three things: what selects it, what it loads first, and where the machine router is.
517: 
518: **The sibling router**: the machine router lives in `ROUTER.md` beside `SKILL.md`, under a final `## MACHINE ROUTER` heading.
519: That heading is the one every reader parses. Its section number is optional, so `## MACHINE ROUTER` and `## 9. MACHINE ROUTER` both count, and the check ignores the number.
520: Keep pseudocode out of SMART ROUTING and put it in that section.
521: `SKILL.md` carries no `## MACHINE ROUTER` section of its own: two homes for one router is the dual declaration the check reports.
522: 
523: **The link line**: Section 2 names the router file with a relative markdown link, [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md), and its target resolves on disk. A sentence that mentions the name without a link fails, because a reader cannot follow it to a file that is not there.
524: 
525: **One router per folder**: every skill and every mode packet owns `ROUTER.md` inside its own folder, linked from its own `SKILL.md`. A router file whose real path leaves the folder is not that skill's router.
526: 
527: **The no-match outcome** is named `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK` everywhere. Low confidence returns a disambiguation checklist, never an empty result and never a guess.
528: 
529: **Validation**: `package_skill.py --strict` reports the routing shape with five codes:
530: 
531: | Code | Finding |
532: |------|---------|
533: | `RS-001` | SMART ROUTING is longer than the limit (12 lines or 180 words by default) |
534: | `RS-002` | `SKILL.md` carries a `## MACHINE ROUTER` section, with or without a code block |
535: | `RS-003` | A `## MACHINE ROUTER` section is not the last H2 of the document that holds it |
536: | `RS-004` | the skill has no sibling `ROUTER.md`, or its real path leaves the skill folder |
537: | `RS-005` | `SKILL.md` has no relative markdown link to `./ROUTER.md` that resolves |
538: 
539: The machine block itself is a fenced block or an unfenced run of indented lines.
540: It declares the router with one of these markers: `INTENT_SIGNALS =`, `RESOURCE_MAP =`, `DEFAULT_RESOURCE =`, `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST =`, `def discover_markdown_resources` or `def _guard_in_skill`.
541: A fence closes only on a run of the same character that is at least as long as its opening run.
542: 
543: **Known debt** is listed in `sk-create-skill/scripts/routing-shape-known-debt.json`.
544: Entries use skill paths relative to `.skilled/skills`, such as `sk-code/sk-code-review`.
545: A folder outside that root is never debt.
546: Each entry records `{"lines", "words", "machineBlocks", "codes"}`.
547: A listed skill fails if its line count, word count or machine blocks left in `SKILL.md` exceed the record, or if it adds an unrecorded code.
548: The checker ignores entries in any other form.
549: Remove an entry when the skill follows the canon.
550: 
551: **Placement**: the SMART ROUTING section sits after Section 1 (WHEN TO USE) and before HOW IT WORKS, and `ROUTER.md` sits beside `SKILL.md` at the skill root.
552: 
553: **Worked example** (a canon Section 2 and its sibling router, nothing else):
554: 
555: \## 2. SMART ROUTING
556: 
557: Use this skill for [domain] work: [trigger 1], [trigger 2], or [trigger 3].
558: The first signal is [project/stack/mode detection], because it picks the knowledge folder before any intent scoring.
559: Load `references/[default].md` first on every run. The other files assume it.
560: Then load what the matched intent maps to: [intent A] reads `references/[domain]/[a].md`, and [intent B] reads `assets/[domain]/[b].md`.
561: Keep every path inside this skill folder and load a file only when it exists.
562: When two intents score close together, follow both in rank order.
563: When nothing matches, report `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK` with the checklist from the machine router instead of guessing.
564: The machine router lives in [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md); read it before selecting a resource.
565: 
566: ---
567: 
568: The link resolves to the sibling file, whose one heading the readers parse is:
569: 
570: \## MACHINE ROUTER
571: 
572: ```python
573: DEFAULT_RESOURCE = "references/[default].md"
574: INTENT_SIGNALS = {"PRIMARY": {"weight": 4, "keywords": [("[keyword]", 4), ("[phrase]", 3)]}}
575: RESOURCE_MAP = {"PRIMARY": ["references/[domain]/[primary].md"]}
576: UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST = ["Confirm the routing key", "Confirm the intent", "Provide one concrete input"]
577: 
578: def route_[skill_name]_resources(user_request, task=None):
579:     inventory = discover_markdown_resources()
580:     primary, secondary, scores = classify_intents(user_request, task)
581:     if max(scores.values() or [0]) < 0.5:
582:         return {"load_level": "UNKNOWN_FALLBACK", "checklist": UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST}
583:     return {"routing_key": get_routing_key(task, [primary]), "resources": inventory}
584: ```
585: 
586: The full resilience pattern (guarded paths, recursive discovery, routing keys) is in [skill-smart-router.md](./skill-smart-router.md).
587: 
588: **Writing Tips**:
589: - Open Section 2 with the signal that actually picks this skill's files.
590: - Name the first file to load, so a reader knows where to start.
591: - Name the router file with a markdown link, so a reader can open it.
592: - Keep `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK` as the named no-match outcome.
593: - Edit `INTENT_SIGNALS` and `RESOURCE_MAP` in `ROUTER.md` when the skill gains a domain.
594: - Avoid duplicate lookup tables, static file inventories, and unguarded `load()` calls.
595: 
596: **Word Budget**: 8-12 non-blank lines of prose

627: **Example**:
628: \`\`\`[language]
629: # Realistic example
630: \`\`\`
631: 
632: **Writing Tips**:
633: - Use Mermaid for flow diagrams so a parser can read them.
634: - Show, don't just tell (include code examples)
635: - Progressive detail: Overview → specifics → edge cases
636: - Link to references for deep dives
637: - **Flowchart Supplements**: Add visual flowcharts before/after complex Python/YAML logic (see below)
638: 
639: **Word Budget**: 150-300 lines
640: 
641: ### Flowchart Supplements (For Complex Logic)
642: 
643: **Purpose**: Add visual clarity to complex Python/YAML logic blocks without removing structured code
644: 
645: **When to Use**:
646: - Complex conditional logic (nested if/else, multiple branches)
647: - Mode detection algorithms
648: - Multi-step decision trees
649: - Workflow routing logic
650: - State machine transitions
651: 
652: **Approach**:
653: - **Supplement, don't replace**: Keep existing Python/YAML code intact
654: - **Add flowcharts**: Place ASCII flowchart before or after code block
655: - **Visual aid purpose**: Help quick understanding of logic flow
656: 
657: **Structure**:
658: 
659: ### [Logic Section Name]
660: 
661: **[Brief explanation of what this logic does]**
662: 
663: **Logic Flow**:
664: \`\`\`
665: START
666:   ↓
667: [Check Condition A]
668:   ↓
669: A True? ─── NO ──→ [Path B]
670:   │                    ↓
671:   │              [Process B]
672:   │                    ↓
673:   YES              [Continue]
674:   ↓
675: [Process A]
676:   ↓
677: RESULT
678: \`\`\`
679: 
680: **Implementation**:
681: \`\`\`python
682: def example_logic(input):
683:     """Original Python logic preserved"""
684:     if condition_a:
685:         return process_a(input)
686:     else:
687:         return process_b(input)
688: \`\`\`
689: 
690: **OR for configuration:**
691: 
692: \`\`\`yaml
693: mode_detection:
694:   trigger_patterns:
695:     ticket: ["$ticket", "create ticket"]
696:     story: ["$story", "user story"]
697:   defaults:
698:     mode: interactive
699:     depth: 10
700: \`\`\`
701: 
702: **Writing Tips**:
703: - **Keep code**: Don't remove Python/YAML - it's precise and complete
704: - **Add diagrams**: Flowcharts provide at-a-glance understanding
705: - **Placement**:
706:   - Flowchart FIRST if it aids comprehension before reading code
707:   - Flowchart AFTER if it summarizes complex code
708:   - Both before AND after for very complex logic
709: - **Consistency**: Use the same ASCII flowchart style as the other diagrams in the file
710: - **When to skip**: Simple 2-3 line logic doesn't need flowcharts
711: 
712: **Example Use Cases**:
713: - Mode detection with 5+ conditions → Flowchart + Python code
714: - YAML configuration with complex triggers → Keep YAML, add decision tree diagram
715: - Multi-step workflow routing → Flowchart showing paths, keep implementation code
716: 
717: **Word Budget**: Variable (adds 10-30 lines per complex logic block)
718: 
719: ---
720: 
721: ### Section 4: RULES (REQUIRED)
722: 
723: **Purpose**: Define mandatory behaviors, prohibited actions, and escalation triggers
724: 
725: **Validation**: package_skill.py requires this section with specific subsections
726: 
727: **Essential Content** (all three subsections REQUIRED):
728: - ALWAYS rules (4-7 critical requirements)
729: - NEVER rules (3-5 anti-patterns to avoid)
730: - ESCALATE IF (3-5 situations requiring user input)
731: 
732: **Structure**:
733: 
734: ### ALWAYS
735: 
736: **ALWAYS do these without asking:**
737: 
738: 1. **ALWAYS [requirement]**
739:    - [Why this matters]
740:    - [Implementation detail]
741: 
742: ### NEVER
743: 
744: **NEVER do these:**
745: 
746: 1. **NEVER [anti-pattern]**
747:    - [Why problematic]
748:    - [Alternative approach]
749: 
750: ### ESCALATE IF
751: 
752: **Ask user when:**
753: 
754: 1. **ESCALATE IF [ambiguous situation]**
755:    - [What's unclear]
756:    - [What clarification needed]
757: 
758: **Writing Tips**:
759: - Use ALL CAPS for subsection headers: `ALWAYS`, `NEVER`, `ESCALATE IF` (or `ESCALATE WHEN`)
760: - Be specific and actionable
761: - Explain *why* for each rule (rationale matters)
762: - Include implementation guidance
763: - Present options to user for ESCALATE IF cases
764: 
765: **Word Budget**: 100-200 lines
766: 
767: ---
768: 
769: ### Section 5: REFERENCES
770: 
771: **Purpose**: Expose the operational references and templates the skill depends on.
772: 
773: **Essential Content**:
774: - Core references used during execution
775: - Templates/assets used during output generation
776: - Loading notes that stay consistent with Section 2 (SMART ROUTING)
777: 
778: **Structure**:
779: 
780: ### Core References
781: - [reference-name.md](./references/reference-name.md) - Primary guidance
782: 
783: ### Templates and Assets
784: - [template-name.md](./assets/template-name.md) - Reusable output template
785: 
786: ### Reference Loading Notes
787: - Load only what current intent requires.
788: - Keep Smart Routing as the single routing authority.
789: 
790: **Word Budget**: 40-120 lines
791: 
792: ---
793: 
794: ### Section 6: SUCCESS CRITERIA
795: 
796: **Purpose**: Define completion conditions and quality standards
797: 
798: **Essential Content**:
799: - Completion checklist (5-10 items)
800: - Quality gates or thresholds
801: - Validation requirements
802: 
803: **Structure**:
804: 
805: ### Task Completion Checklist
806: 
807: **[Workflow name] Complete When:**
808: 
809: - [ ] [Success criterion 1]
810: - [ ] [Success criterion 2]
811: - [ ] [Success criterion 3]
812: 
813: ### Quality Gates
814: 
815: **Before marking complete:**
816: 
817: - **[Dimension]**: [Specific requirement]
818: - **[Dimension]**: [Specific requirement]
819: 
820: **Writing Tips**:
821: - Use checkbox format `- [ ]` for checklists
822: - Specific and measurable criteria
823: - Include both completion and quality checks
824: - Define thresholds numerically where possible
825: 
826: **Word Budget**: 50-120 lines
827: 
828: ---
829: 
830: ### Section 7: INTEGRATION POINTS
831: 
832: **Purpose**: Document how skill integrates with systems, tools, and workflow contracts
833: 
834: **Essential Content**:
835: - Validation workflow integration
836: - Required workflow contracts and handoff rules
837: - Tool usage patterns
838: - Knowledge base dependencies
839: - External tool requirements
840: 
841: **Structure**:
842: 
843: ### Validation Workflow Integration
844: 
845: **[Validation Name]**:
846: - Triggers: [When to run]
847: - Purpose: [What it validates]
848: 
849: ### Cross-Workflow Contracts
850: 
851: **[Contract Name]**: [When it applies and what the skill must hand off]
852: 
853: ### Tool Usage Guidelines
854: 
855: **[Tool]**: [Usage pattern]
856: 
857: ### Knowledge Base Dependencies
858: 
859: - **Required**: [Files needed]
860: - **Optional**: [Enhancing files]
861: 
862: ### External Tools
863: 
864: **[Tool Name]**:
865: - Installation: [How]
866: - Purpose: [Why]
867: 
868: **Writing Tips**:
869: - Distinguish required vs. optional dependencies
870: - Provide installation/setup instructions for external tools
871: - Explain fallback behavior if optional resources missing
872: - Link related skills by name
873: 
874: **Word Budget**: 50-150 lines
875: 
876: ---
877: 
878: ## 5. COMMON PITFALLS
879: 
880: For the complete list of 8 common pitfalls with before/after examples, see:
881: → **[common-pitfalls.md](../../references/shared/common-pitfalls.md)**
882: 
883: **Quick Summary:**
884: 1. Generic descriptions → Be specific about capabilities
885: 2. Bloated SKILL.md → Move details to references/
886: 3. Missing bundled resources → Identify repeated code/docs
887: 4. Unclear triggers → Specific activation conditions
888: 5. Distant instructions → Use the [Prose Clarity Checklist](../../references/skill/creation-workflow.md#prose-clarity-checklist)
889: 6. Platform-specific claims → Stay platform-agnostic
890: 7. Multiline YAML descriptions → Keep single line
891: 8. Redundant routing tables → Keep routing authority in pseudocode
892: 
893: ### Writing Style Quick Reference
894: 
895: For instructions and README prose, use the [Prose Clarity Checklist](../../references/skill/creation-workflow.md#prose-clarity-checklist).
896: 
897: ---
898: 
899: ## 6. QUALITY CHECKLIST & QUICK REFERENCE
900: 
901: ### Pre-Packaging Checklist
902: 
903: **Before running package_skill.py:**
904: 
905: Frontmatter:
906: □ YAML frontmatter present and valid
907: □ Required fields: name, description, allowed-tools
908: □ Name is hyphen-case (matches directory)
909: □ Description uses third-person voice
910: □ Description is specific (not generic)
911: □ No angle brackets in description
912: □ allowed-tools lists all tools used
913: 
914: Structure:
915: □ H1 title with descriptive subtitle
916: □ Numbered H2 sections for the body (1. WHEN TO USE, 2. SMART ROUTING, etc.)
917: □ H2 headings use ALL CAPS
918: □ Section separators (---) between major sections
919: □ No table of contents (forbidden in SKILL.md)
920: □ Proper heading hierarchy (H1 → H2 → H3)
921: □ SMART ROUTING section placed after WHEN TO USE, before HOW IT WORKS
922: 
923: Content - Standard Sections:
924: □ WHEN TO USE section includes use cases + anti-patterns
925: □ HOW IT WORKS section explains workflow clearly
926: □ RULES section has ALWAYS, NEVER, ESCALATE IF
927: □ REFERENCES section lists core references/templates explicitly
928: □ SUCCESS CRITERIA section defines completion
929: □ INTEGRATION POINTS section documents dependencies
930: □ All bundled resources referenced from SKILL.md
931: □ No duplication between SKILL.md and references/
932: 
933: Content - Routing Canon:
934: □ Section 1 (WHEN TO USE) contains ONLY activation triggers and use cases
935: □ Section 1 does NOT contain file-path routing logic
936: □ SMART ROUTING section exists (Section 2 - REQUIRED for all skills)
937: □ Section 2 is 8-12 non-blank lines of plain prose: what selects this skill, what it loads first, where the machine router is
938: □ Section 2 names the no-match outcome `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK`
939: □ Any machine router block sits in the sibling `ROUTER.md`, never inside SMART ROUTING
940: □ `SKILL.md` carries no `## MACHINE ROUTER` section of its own
941: □ Section 2 links to [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md) with a relative markdown link that resolves
942: □ `ROUTER.md` sits beside `SKILL.md`, and every path in it stays inside the skill folder
943: □ Flowchart supplements added to complex logic blocks in Section 3 (where applicable)
944: □ Python/YAML code preserved (supplements, not replacements)
945: □ Mermaid diagrams use valid syntax (when used)
946: 
947: Quality:
948: □ SKILL.md under 5k words (<3k preferred)
949: □ Concrete examples included
950: □ Rationale provided for rules
951: □ Instructions follow the [Prose Clarity Checklist](../../references/skill/creation-workflow.md#prose-clarity-checklist)
952: □ Consistent heading format
953: □ All code blocks specify language
954: □ Links work correctly
955: □ Section 1 contains ONLY triggers/use cases (NO file references)
956: □ `MACHINE ROUTER` pseudocode guards every path and checks that the file exists

960: | Element               | Requirement                | Example                                                                                            |
961: | --------------------- | -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |

14: # SKILL.md File Templates - Creation Guide
15: 
16: Templates for creating SKILL.md files with proper structure, frontmatter, and required sections.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Purpose of SKILL.md Files
23: 
24: SKILL.md files define AI agent skills - reusable capabilities that extend an agent's functionality for specific domains or workflows. A well-crafted SKILL.md:
25: 
26: - **Triggers automatically** when relevant patterns are detected
27: - **Guides the agent** through specialized workflows
28: - **Maintains consistency** across conversations
29: - **Encodes expertise** in specific domains
30: 
31: ### Template Overview
32: 
33: This guide provides **one comprehensive SKILL template** (Section 3) that covers all skill types from simple single-purpose tools to complex multi-mode orchestrators.
34: 
35: **The template is flexible:**
36: - **Simple skills**: Use required core sections only (WHEN TO USE, SMART ROUTING, HOW IT WORKS, RULES, REFERENCES)
37: - **Skills with bundled resources**: Say in Section 2 what selects the skill and what it loads first, and put the router in the sibling `ROUTER.md`. Use `references/`, `assets/`, and `scripts/`
38: - **Multi-mode skills**: Expand WHEN TO USE and HOW IT WORKS sections by mode
39: - **All skills**: Section 2 (SMART ROUTING) is required: 8 to 12 non-blank lines of plain prose
40: 
41: **Target size**: 800-2000 lines for SKILL.md (<5k words total)
42: 
43: **Examples**:
44: - Simple: Unit test generator, documentation formatter (no bundled resources)
45: - Moderate: API client, specialized code reviewer (with references and assets)
46: - Complex: Workflow orchestrator, document quality pipeline (multi-mode with extensive resources)
47: 
48: ### Progressive Disclosure Principle
49: 
50: SKILL.md architecture follows progressive disclosure:
51: 
52: 1. **Metadata** (YAML frontmatter) - Always in context (~100 words)
53: 2. **SKILL.md body** - When skill activates (<5k words)
54: 3. **Bundled resources** - Loaded as needed (unlimited size)
55: 
56: **Critical**: Keep SKILL.md <5k words. Move detailed content to `references/`, `scripts/`, or `assets/`.
57: 
58: ### Document Type Requirements
59: 
60: **Enforcement Level**: STRICT (SKILL.md files require perfect structure)
61: 
62: **Required Elements**:
63: - ✅ YAML frontmatter with required fields
64: - ✅ H1 title with subtitle
65: - ✅ Numbered H2 sections (ALL CAPS, integers only, never a letter suffix such as `2b.`)
66: - ✅ Section separators (`---`)
67: - ✅ No table of contents (forbidden in SKILL.md)
68: 
69: **Quality Targets**:
70: - Structure: 100/100
71: - Content quality: High (AI-evaluated)
72: - Overall: High (human/AI judgment)
73: 
74: ---
75: 
76: ## 2. FRONTMATTER REQUIREMENTS
77: 
78: ### Required Fields
79: 
80: | Field | Required | Format | Example |
81: |-------|----------|--------|---------|
82: | `name` | ✅ | hyphen-case | `my-skill-name` |
83: | `description` | ✅ | Single line, **≤ 130 chars** for skills (≤ 110 for commands), 1,536-char hard cap | `"Handles X when Y occurs"` |
84: | `allowed-tools` | ✅ | Array: `[Tool1, Tool2]` | `[Read, Write, Edit, Bash]` |
85: | `version` | ✅ | 4-part X.Y.Z.W | `1.0.0.0` |
86: 
87: > **Hard rules**: not a frontmatter key. They live in `hard-rules.json` beside the skill's `SKILL.md`, a JSON array of `{id, check, message, severity}` objects that the dispatch preflight reads.
88: 
89: > **Description budget & trim style**: see [`frontmatter-templates.md` § Description Budget & Trim Style](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md).
90: > Keep total project descriptions under the ~6,400-character ceiling. This leaves headroom below the 8,000-character auto-discovery limit.
91: > Drop product and stack lists. Drop marketing prose. Keep the skill name, primary verb, domain noun and mode suffixes (`:auto` or `:confirm`).
92: 
93: ### Template
94: 
95: ```yaml
96: ---
97: name: sk-example
98: description: Example workflow skill demonstrating proper frontmatter format with specific capabilities, use cases, and key differentiators for AI agent discovery.
99: allowed-tools: [Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob, Grep]
100: version: 1.0.0.0
101: ---
102: ```
103: 
104: ### Key Rules
105: 
106: - **name**: Must match folder name exactly, hyphen-case only
107: - **description**: Third-person voice, single line, no `<>` brackets
108: - **allowed-tools**: Use brackets `[...]`, not comma-separated string
109: - **hard rules**: Not a frontmatter key. They live in `hard-rules.json` beside `SKILL.md`, a JSON array of `{id, check, message, severity}` objects the dispatch preflight reads.
110: 
111: > **Complete Reference**: For validation rules, edge cases, array formats, and all document type frontmatter, see [frontmatter-templates.md](../../../sk-create-frontmatter/assets/frontmatter-templates.md)
112: 
113: ---
114: 
115: ## 3. SKILL TEMPLATE (WITH BUNDLED RESOURCES)
116: 
117: **Use for**: Skills with bundled resources (references, scripts, or assets)
118: 
119: **Target**: 800-2000 lines (SKILL.md <1000 lines, rest in resources)
120: 
121: **Size Constraints** (package_skill.py validation):
122: - Max 5000 words (3000 recommended)
123: - Max 3000 lines
124: 
125: **Required Sections**: WHEN TO USE, SMART ROUTING, HOW IT WORKS, RULES (with ✅ ALWAYS, ❌ NEVER, ⚠️ ESCALATE IF), REFERENCES (or combined `SMART ROUTING & REFERENCES`)
126: 
127: Packaging enforcement note:
128: - `package_skill.py` fails if `REFERENCES` is missing and no approved combined `SMART ROUTING & REFERENCES` structure exists.
129: 
130: **Recommended Sections**: SUCCESS CRITERIA, INTEGRATION POINTS, REFERENCES AND RELATED RESOURCES
131: 
132: ### Template
133: 
134: ```yaml
135: ---
136: name: example-skill
137: description: Example skill demonstrating proper template structure with specific capabilities for semantic code search and context preservation workflows.
138: allowed-tools: [Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Glob, Grep]
139: version: 1.0.0.0
140: ---
141: ```

188: \## 2. SMART ROUTING

191: The first signal is [project/stack/mode detection], because it picks the knowledge folder before any intent scoring.
192: Load `references/[default].md` first on every run. It holds the baseline rules the other files assume.
193: Then load what the matched intent maps to: [intent A] reads `references/[domain]/[a].md`, and [intent B] reads `assets/[domain]/[b].md`.

195: When two intents score close together, follow both in rank order.
196: When nothing matches, report `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK` with the checklist from the machine router instead of guessing.
197: The machine router lives in [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md). Read it before selecting a resource; the pseudocode stays there, not here.

413: - Section 1 (WHEN TO USE): 150-200 lines
414: - Section 2 (SMART ROUTING): 8-12 non-blank lines of plain prose (the router block lives in the sibling `ROUTER.md`)
415: - Section 3 (HOW IT WORKS): 200-300 lines

417: - Section 5 (REFERENCES): 40-120 lines
418: - Section 6 (SUCCESS CRITERIA): 80-120 lines
419: - Section 7 (INTEGRATION POINTS): 100-150 lines
420: - Section 8 (REFERENCES AND RELATED RESOURCES): 20-60 lines

422: **Bundled Resources Structure (Monolithic)**:
423: ```
424: .skilled/skills/skill-name/       # Note: .skilled/skills/ (singular, NOT skills)
425: ├── SKILL.md (800-1000 lines)
426: └── Bundled Resources
427:     ├── scripts/          - Executable automation
428:     ├── references/       - Detailed documentation (flat or domain subfolders)
429:     └── assets/           - Templates and examples (subfolders OK)
430:         ├── opencode/     - OpenCode component templates (skills, agents, commands)
431:         └── readme/        - README-shaped scaffolds (README, install guide)
432: ```

434: **Folder Organization Principle**:
435: - **references/** = flat for small skills, domain subfolders for medium/complex skills
436:   - Flat example: `references/core-standards.md`, `references/validation.md`
437:   - Domain example: `references/backend/go/`, `references/frontend/react/`
438: - **assets/** = Subfolders ALLOWED when organizing many files by category
439:   - Group related templates together
440:   - Example: `assets/skill/`, `assets/readme/`, `assets/flowcharts/`
441: - **scripts/** = Typically flat, but subfolders OK for large script collections

443: **Native Discovery**:
444: - Skills auto-discovered from `.skilled/skills/*/SKILL.md` frontmatter
445: - Skill name in frontmatter MUST match folder name
446: - Skills appear as `skills_<name>` functions in OpenCode (hyphens → underscores)
447: - Invoke via `Read(".skilled/skills/<name>/SKILL.md")`

504: ### Section 2: SMART ROUTING (Required for All Skills)
505: 
506: **Purpose**: Use this section to explain how you route a request to this skill's resources.
507: 
508: **Three skill kinds, one shape**:
509: 
510: | Kind | How to tell | What Section 2 says |
511: |------|-------------|---------------------|
512: | Hub | the folder holds `mode-registry.json` and `hub-router.json` | how a prompt reaches a mode, and where the root `ROUTER.md` is |
513: | Mode packet | a packet folder inside a hub | what selects this packet, what it loads first, and where its own `ROUTER.md` is |
514: | Standalone | neither hub file | the same as a mode packet, with the router in its own `ROUTER.md` |
515: 
516: **The limit**: 12 non-blank lines and 180 words are the hard ceilings the check enforces. Aim for 8 to 12 lines. A packet or standalone skill says three things: what selects it, what it loads first, and where the machine router is.
517: 
518: **The sibling router**: the machine router lives in `ROUTER.md` beside `SKILL.md`, under a final `## MACHINE ROUTER` heading.
519: That heading is the one every reader parses. Its section number is optional, so `## MACHINE ROUTER` and `## 9. MACHINE ROUTER` both count, and the check ignores the number.
520: Keep pseudocode out of SMART ROUTING and put it in that section.
521: `SKILL.md` carries no `## MACHINE ROUTER` section of its own: two homes for one router is the dual declaration the check reports.
522: 
523: **The link line**: Section 2 names the router file with a relative markdown link, [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md), and its target resolves on disk. A sentence that mentions the name without a link fails, because a reader cannot follow it to a file that is not there.
524: 
525: **One router per folder**: every skill and every mode packet owns `ROUTER.md` inside its own folder, linked from its own `SKILL.md`. A router file whose real path leaves the folder is not that skill's router.
526: 
527: **The no-match outcome** is named `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK` everywhere. Low confidence returns a disambiguation checklist, never an empty result and never a guess.
528: 
529: **Validation**: `package_skill.py --strict` reports the routing shape with five codes:
530: 
531: | Code | Finding |
532: |------|---------|
533: | `RS-001` | SMART ROUTING is longer than the limit (12 lines or 180 words by default) |
534: | `RS-002` | `SKILL.md` carries a `## MACHINE ROUTER` section, with or without a code block |
535: | `RS-003` | A `## MACHINE ROUTER` section is not the last H2 of the document that holds it |
536: | `RS-004` | the skill has no sibling `ROUTER.md`, or its real path leaves the skill folder |
537: | `RS-005` | `SKILL.md` has no relative markdown link to `./ROUTER.md` that resolves |
538: 
539: The machine block itself is a fenced block or an unfenced run of indented lines.
540: It declares the router with one of these markers: `INTENT_SIGNALS =`, `RESOURCE_MAP =`, `DEFAULT_RESOURCE =`, `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST =`, `def discover_markdown_resources` or `def _guard_in_skill`.
541: A fence closes only on a run of the same character that is at least as long as its opening run.
542: 
543: **Known debt** is listed in `sk-create-skill/scripts/routing-shape-known-debt.json`.
544: Entries use skill paths relative to `.skilled/skills`, such as `sk-code/sk-code-review`.
545: A folder outside that root is never debt.
546: Each entry records `{"lines", "words", "machineBlocks", "codes"}`.
547: A listed skill fails if its line count, word count or machine blocks left in `SKILL.md` exceed the record, or if it adds an unrecorded code.
548: The checker ignores entries in any other form.
549: Remove an entry when the skill follows the canon.
550: 
551: **Placement**: the SMART ROUTING section sits after Section 1 (WHEN TO USE) and before HOW IT WORKS, and `ROUTER.md` sits beside `SKILL.md` at the skill root.
552: 
553: **Worked example** (a canon Section 2 and its sibling router, nothing else):
554: 
555: \## 2. SMART ROUTING
556: 
557: Use this skill for [domain] work: [trigger 1], [trigger 2], or [trigger 3].
558: The first signal is [project/stack/mode detection], because it picks the knowledge folder before any intent scoring.
559: Load `references/[default].md` first on every run. The other files assume it.
560: Then load what the matched intent maps to: [intent A] reads `references/[domain]/[a].md`, and [intent B] reads `assets/[domain]/[b].md`.
561: Keep every path inside this skill folder and load a file only when it exists.
562: When two intents score close together, follow both in rank order.
563: When nothing matches, report `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK` with the checklist from the machine router instead of guessing.
564: The machine router lives in [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md); read it before selecting a resource.
565: 
566: ---
567: 
568: The link resolves to the sibling file, whose one heading the readers parse is:
569: 
570: \## MACHINE ROUTER
571: 
572: ```python
573: DEFAULT_RESOURCE = "references/[default].md"
574: INTENT_SIGNALS = {"PRIMARY": {"weight": 4, "keywords": [("[keyword]", 4), ("[phrase]", 3)]}}
575: RESOURCE_MAP = {"PRIMARY": ["references/[domain]/[primary].md"]}
576: UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST = ["Confirm the routing key", "Confirm the intent", "Provide one concrete input"]
577: 
578: def route_[skill_name]_resources(user_request, task=None):
579:     inventory = discover_markdown_resources()
580:     primary, secondary, scores = classify_intents(user_request, task)
581:     if max(scores.values() or [0]) < 0.5:
582:         return {"load_level": "UNKNOWN_FALLBACK", "checklist": UNKNOWN_FALLBACK_CHECKLIST}
583:     return {"routing_key": get_routing_key(task, [primary]), "resources": inventory}
584: ```
585: 
586: The full resilience pattern (guarded paths, recursive discovery, routing keys) is in [skill-smart-router.md](./skill-smart-router.md).
587: 
588: **Writing Tips**:
589: - Open Section 2 with the signal that actually picks this skill's files.
590: - Name the first file to load, so a reader knows where to start.
591: - Name the router file with a markdown link, so a reader can open it.
592: - Keep `UNKNOWN_FALLBACK` as the named no-match outcome.
593: - Edit `INTENT_SIGNALS` and `RESOURCE_MAP` in `ROUTER.md` when the skill gains a domain.
594: - Avoid duplicate lookup tables, static file inventories, and unguarded `load()` calls.
595: 
596: **Word Budget**: 8-12 non-blank lines of prose

31: ## 2. OVERVIEW
32: 
33: ### Why This Skill Exists
34: 
35: When a plan carries real trade-offs, one AI answer is one confident guess with no record of what it ruled out. You can hand-run "ask three models" but you get diversity without a convergence rule, no persistence and no audit trail. You need structured disagreement: seats that propose independently, critique each other and only agree when the evidence supports it, not when politeness demands it. You also need a replayable record of every round so your team can see why a plan won, not just what won.
36: 
37: ### What It Does
38: 
39: `deep-ai-council` runs a planning-only multi-seat council. Two or three seats, each with a distinct reasoning lens from six available (Analytical, Creative, Critical, Pragmatic, Holistic, Research), propose independently. Then three critique roles (Hunter, Skeptic and Referee) attack the leading plan before anything is declared settled. Convergence follows a two-of-three rule: two seats must agree on the material plan and critique must find no new high-severity blocker. The council never implements. It hands the recommended plan plus the full artifact trail to you or your implementation agent.

90: ## 4. HOW IT WORKS
91: 
92: ### The Council Round
93: 
94: A council run moves through three steps. First, resolve the target packet folder and select 2-3 seats, each assigned a distinct reasoning lens. When real external executors are available you can add a different AI vantage in a second round, but all seats inside one round always use the same CLI. Simulated vantages stay labeled as simulated. The default and most common run is a single in-CLI round. Add external rounds only when a fresh vantage adds value.
95: 
96: Second, deliberate. Each seat proposes independently. Then the adversarial critique pass tries to break the leading proposal before agreement is allowed. If the council hits its round cap without convergence, the run completes as non-converged rather than fabricating consensus. Non-converged is an honest answer: it means the evidence did not settle toward one plan.
97: 
98: Third, persist and hand off. The council produces a report with sections mandated by the output schema and writes the canonical packet-local `ai-council/` artifacts when running as the scoped-write agent. The CLI helper is a fallback for non-council callers with a captured report. Failed rounds move under `failed/` so the forensic trail survives. Implementation passes to an implementation agent or the caller.
99: 
100: ### Six Strategy Lenses
101: 
102: Each seat draws from one of six lenses so no two seats repeat the same reasoning path. Analytical decomposes the problem into components and dependencies. Creative explores unconventional shapes. Critical pressure-tests failure modes and edge cases. Pragmatic scores for implementation cost and incremental value. Holistic checks system fit and long-range consequences. Research gathers external evidence and tests source quality.
103: 
104: A round uses 2 or 3 seats and never more. The task type drives the lens recommendation: a bug fix benefits from analytical, critical and pragmatic. A feature call benefits from creative, analytical and holistic.
105: 
106: ### Three Critique Roles
107: 
108: Before convergence is allowed, three roles test the leading plan. The Hunter attacks for missed edge cases and weak evidence. The Skeptic defends, separating real flaws from intended trade-offs. The Referee adjusts scores based on both arguments and records the adjustments so the reasoning stays auditable. No plan passes without surviving this pass.
109: 
110: ### The Two-of-Three Convergence Rule
111: 
112: Convergence is not a popularity vote. A plan converges when two of three seats agree on the material direction and the critique pass finds no new high-severity blocker. The shipped config also declares the shared anti-convergence floor for council mode: `antiConvergence.minRounds = 2`, `convergenceMode = "default"` and `stopPolicy = "fail-closed"`. If the council hits `max_rounds` without hitting that bar, the run emits `non-converged`. Preserved failed-round forensics let you inspect what blocked convergence and decide whether to add a round, change lenses or accept the partial result.

119: 
120: Reach for the council when a plan has real trade-offs and you want structured disagreement rather than one person's (or one model's) best guess. It fits architecture decisions, multi-path refactors, high-risk changes and any situation where knowing what got ruled out matters as much as what won.
121: 
122: Skip it when the question has one clear answer, when you need a quick implementation path without comparison or when the extra cost of 2-3 seat runs is not justified.
123: 
124: The council is planning only. It recommends a plan and persists the reasoning. It never writes application code, never edits spec docs outside `ai-council/` and never commits or deploys. Once it hands off, implementation belongs to `@code`, the caller or your own workflow.

161: ## 7. FAQ
162: 
163: **Q: Does the council implement the plan it recommends?**
164: 
165: A: No. It produces planning artifacts and hands off. Implementation belongs to `@code`, the caller or your own workflow. The council never writes application code, never edits spec docs outside `ai-council/` and never commits.
166: 
167: **Q: When should I use a council instead of asking one model for a plan?**
168: 
169: A: Use a single model when the direction is clear. Use the council when the trade-offs are real, when you need to know what was ruled out and why or when the decision will be hard to reverse later. The council costs more compute but produces a disagreement record a single model cannot give you.
170: 
171: **Q: What does the two-of-three rule actually mean?**
172: 
173: A: Two of three seats must agree on the material plan direction, and the critique pass must find no new high-severity blocker. If critique surfaces a blocker, the leading plan is not converged regardless of seat agreement. The rule prevents both false consensus and popularity contests.
174:

Deliberations and critiques live in their own folders. Failed rounds move under `failed/`. Nothing is deleted, and nothing is rewritten.

Convergence follows a two-of-three rule: two seats must agree on the material plan and critique must find no new high-severity blocker. The council never implements. It hands the recommended plan plus the full artifact trail to you or your implementation agent.

90: ## 4. HOW IT WORKS
91: 
92: ### The Council Round
93: 
94: A council run moves through three steps. First, resolve the target packet folder and select 2-3 seats, each assigned a distinct reasoning lens. When real external executors are available you can add a different AI vantage in a second round, but all seats inside one round always use the same CLI. Simulated vantages stay labeled as simulated. The default and most common run is a single in-CLI round. Add external rounds only when a fresh vantage adds value.
95: 
96: Second, deliberate. Each seat proposes independently. Then the adversarial critique pass tries to break the leading proposal before agreement is allowed. If the council hits its round cap without convergence, the run completes as non-converged rather than fabricating consensus. Non-converged is an honest answer: it means the evidence did not settle toward one plan.
97: 
98: Third, persist and hand off. The council produces a report with sections mandated by the output schema and writes the canonical packet-local `ai-council/` artifacts when running as the scoped-write agent. The CLI helper is a fallback for non-council callers with a captured report. Failed rounds move under `failed/` so the forensic trail survives. Implementation passes to an implementation agent or the caller.
99: 
100: ### Six Strategy Lenses
101: 
102: Each seat draws from one of six lenses so no two seats repeat the same reasoning path. Analytical decomposes the problem into components and dependencies. Creative explores unconventional shapes. Critical pressure-tests failure modes and edge cases. Pragmatic scores for implementation cost and incremental value. Holistic checks system fit and long-range consequences. Research gathers external evidence and tests source quality.
103: 
104: A round uses 2 or 3 seats and never more. The task type drives the lens recommendation: a bug fix benefits from analytical, critical and pragmatic. A feature call benefits from creative, analytical and holistic.
105: 
106: ### Three Critique Roles
107: 
108: Before convergence is allowed, three roles test the leading plan. The Hunter attacks for missed edge cases and weak evidence. The Skeptic defends, separating real flaws from intended trade-offs. The Referee adjusts scores based on both arguments and records the adjustments so the reasoning stays auditable. No plan passes without surviving this pass.
109: 
110: ### The Two-of-Three Convergence Rule
111: 
112: Convergence is not a popularity vote. A plan converges when two of three seats agree on the material direction and the critique pass finds no new high-severity blocker. The shipped config also declares the shared anti-convergence floor for council mode: `antiConvergence.minRounds = 2`, `convergenceMode = "default"` and `stopPolicy = "fail-closed"`. If the council hits `max_rounds` without hitting that bar, the run emits `non-converged`. Preserved failed-round forensics let you inspect what blocked convergence and decide whether to add a round, change lenses or accept the partial result.
113:

116: ## 5. INTEGRATION & NAVIGATION
117: 
118: ### When To Use This Skill
119: 
120: Reach for the council when a plan has real trade-offs and you want structured disagreement rather than one person's (or one model's) best guess. It fits architecture decisions, multi-path refactors, high-risk changes and any situation where knowing what got ruled out matters as much as what won.
121: 
122: Skip it when the question has one clear answer, when you need a quick implementation path without comparison or when the extra cost of 2-3 seat runs is not justified.
123: 
124: The council is planning only. It recommends a plan and persists the reasoning. It never writes application code, never edits spec docs outside `ai-council/` and never commits or deploys. Once it hands off, implementation belongs to `@code`, the caller or your own workflow.

149: 
150: | What you see | Why | Fix |
151: |---|---|---|
152: | Council emits `non-converged` | The council hit `max_rounds` without two-of-three agreement and refused to fake consensus | Read the failed-round forensics under `failed/round-NNN-<timestamp>/`. Add a round with different lenses or accept the partial result as the honest answer. |

154: | Per-seat files are absent from a persisted run | The report used a composition-table fallback instead of per-seat headings | Confirm the report uses valid per-seat headings or a composition table the parser accepts. |
155: | Seats produce nearly identical proposals | Seat diversity was too low and the council repeated the same reasoning path | Assign distinct lenses per seat. Check the task-type-to-lens mapping in `references/patterns/seat-diversity-patterns.md` and re-run with more divergent seats. |
156: | `advise-council-completion.cjs` reports no `council_complete` event | The final event was never appended to the state log | Re-open the council context and append the completion event, or re-persist from a completed report. |
157: | Advisor does not route "ai council" prompts | Stale or missing skill graph | Rebuild the skill-advisor graph, then retry the routing query. |

161: ## 7. FAQ
162: 
163: **Q: Does the council implement the plan it recommends?**
164: 
165: A: No. It produces planning artifacts and hands off. Implementation belongs to `@code`, the caller or your own workflow. The council never writes application code, never edits spec docs outside `ai-council/` and never commits.
166: 
167: **Q: When should I use a council instead of asking one model for a plan?**
168: 
169: A: Use a single model when the direction is clear. Use the council when the trade-offs are real, when you need to know what was ruled out and why or when the decision will be hard to reverse later. The council costs more compute but produces a disagreement record a single model cannot give you.
170: 
171: **Q: What does the two-of-three rule actually mean?**
172: 
173: A: Two of three seats must agree on the material plan direction, and the critique pass must find no new high-severity blocker. If critique surfaces a blocker, the leading plan is not converged regardless of seat agreement. The rule prevents both false consensus and popularity contests.
174: 
175: **Q: Where does the audit trail live?**
176: 
177: A: Inside your packet folder under `ai-council/`. The append-only `ai-council-state.jsonl` records every event. Per-seat proposals live under `seats/round-NNN/`. Deliberations and critiques live in their own folders. Failed rounds move under `failed/`. Nothing is deleted, and nothing is rewritten.
178: 
179: **Q: Can I run a council with seats from different AI providers in the same round?**
180: 
181: A: No. All seats inside one round must use the same CLI executor. Seat diversity within a round comes from different models or reasoning lenses on that CLI, not from mixing providers. If you want a different provider's vantage, add a second dedicated round. This keeps each round's sandbox, tool surface and output schema consistent.
182: 
183: **Q: What happens when the council does not converge?**
184: 
185: A: The run completes as `non-converged`. This is an honest answer: the evidence did not settle toward one plan. The failed-round forensics show you what blocked convergence. You can inspect them, adjust lenses or the scope and re-run, or accept the partial result and decide yourself.

18: The council is **primarily an IN-CLI capability**.
19: When you invoke it from inside an active runtime (OpenCode, Claude Code, OpenCode), the council deliberates using THAT runtime's own models and reasoning lenses as seats.
20: No external dispatch is required for the common case.

30: 
31: **Both modes obey the one-CLI-per-round invariant** (§5 ALWAYS rule 6):
32: - In-CLI round: all seats use the current runtime's models.
33: - External-CLI round: all seats use ONE supported external CLI (e.g. all `cli-opencode` seats with different reasoning levels, or all `cli-cursor`, `cli-devin`, `cli-pi`, or `cli-hermes` seats with different models).
34: - Cross-CLI deliberation is staged as MULTIPLE rounds (one in-CLI + one external, or two different externals) — never folded into the same round.

236: - `assets/deep-ai-council-dashboard.md` - council status dashboard template.
237: - `assets/deep-ai-council-config.json` - run-config template for council sessions.
238: - `assets/prompt-pack-round.md` - council seat prompt-pack template.
239: - `assets/runtime-capabilities.json` - runtime parity and validation matrix.
240: - `manual-testing-playbook/manual-testing-playbook.md` - operator validation scenarios.
241: - `README.md` - human-facing overview.
242: 
243: Related skills: `deep-research` for evidence-first investigation vantages and `system-spec-kit` for packet documentation, validation, resume, and memory continuity.
244: 
245: ---
246: 
247: ## 7. SUCCESS CRITERIA
248: 
249: ### Council Skill Completion Checklist
250: 
251: Council alignment is complete when:
252: 
253: - ✅ Council requests route to the `deep-ai-council` advisor/packet surface (`packetSkillName` and `legacyAdvisorId` in `mode-registry.json`); `deep-ai-council` is the packet folder/SKILL.md name (folder == name), while the dispatched agent identity remains `ai-council`.
254: - ✅ Runtime mirrors dispatch `@ai-council` (`mode: subagent`, Task-dispatch only) under a consistent agent identity — both agent files (`.skilled/agents/ai-council.md`, `.claude/agents/ai-council.md`) declare `name: ai-council`, matching the registry `agent: ai-council` field.
255: - ✅ Council references and scripts live inside this skill package.
256: - ✅ Persisted artifacts and append-only state stay under packet-local `ai-council/**`.
257: - ✅ Persistence helpers parse and write the existing council artifact contract while graph support remains a derived projection.
258: 
259: ### Quality Targets
260: 
261: - **Structure**: SKILL.md follows sk-doc required section order and frontmatter.
262: - **Routing**: the SMART ROUTING section and its [`ROUTER.md`](./ROUTER.md) router are the only authoritative routing source.
263: - **Reference shape**: reference filenames are snake_case and intro sections are short.
264: - **Playbook coverage**: manual testing package has 32 scenarios across 9 categories.
265: - **Boundary discipline**: graph rows never replace `ai-council/**` artifacts and council seats do not mutate graph storage directly.
266: 
267: ### Validation Success
268: 
269: - ✅ `quick_validate.py` accepts the skill package.
270: - ✅ The skill's packet spec docs pass `validate.sh --strict`.
271: - ✅ Old kebab-case reference links are absent from live callers.
272: 
273: ---
274: 
275: ## 8. INTEGRATION POINTS
276: 
277: ### Validation Workflow Integration
278: 
279: Run `bash .skilled/skills/system-spec-kit/runtime/cli/spec/validate.sh <spec-folder> --strict` before completion claims when spec docs are updated. Skill package structure is checked with `python3 .skilled/skills/sk-doc/scripts/quick_validate.py .skilled/skills/system-deep-loop/deep-ai-council`.
280: 
281: ### Cross-Workflow Contracts
282: 
283: The council is a planning LEAF. It hands recommendations, risk analysis, and packet-local artifacts to implementation agents or the top-level caller; it does not perform application-code or spec-doc mutations.
284: 
285: ### Tool Usage
286: 
287: - `Read`, `Glob`, and `Grep` gather evidence and verify paths.
288: - `Write` and `Edit` are allowed only for the planning LEAF's packet-local `ai-council/**` artifacts.
289: - `Bash` is for caller-owned helper invocation and validation, not for seat implementation.
290: 
291: ### Knowledge Base Dependencies
292: 
293: **Required**:
294: 
295: - `references/structure/output-schema.md` - parser and report requiredness contract; persistence must fail closed if missing.
296: 
297: **Optional**:
298: 
299: - `references/patterns/command-wiring.md` - caller post-dispatch examples.
300: - `references/convergence/convergence-signals.md` - convergence guidance.
301: - `references/scoring/scoring-rubric.md` - synthesis scoring and critique guidance.
302: - `references/convergence/depth-dispatch.md` - adaptive dispatch guidance.
303: - `references/convergence/failure-handling.md` - failure and rollback treatment.
304: - `references/patterns/anti-patterns.md` - quality anti-pattern detection and recovery.
305: - `references/integration/graph-support.md` - derived graph support and runtime/ CLI boundary.
306: - `references/structure/folder-layout.md` - artifact shape and rollback layout.
307: - `references/patterns/seat-diversity-patterns.md` - lens selection.
308: - `references/structure/state-format.md` - state event semantics.
309: - `manual-testing-playbook/manual-testing-playbook.md` - operator validation.
310: 
311: ### External Tools
312: 
313: No external tools are required. External CLIs may contribute seats only when the caller actually runs them and labels the result accurately.

15: # README Types and Voice
16: 
17: Overflow detail behind `SKILL.md` Section 4 (README authoring). Use it to choose a README type and set the writing voice before drafting sections.
18: 
19: ---
20: 
21: ## 1. OVERVIEW
22: 
23: ### Purpose
24: 
25: A README answers "What is this?" and "How do I use it?" in a scannable, progressive format. The type and voice decisions below shape every section that follows, so make them before copying a template.
26: 
27: The README type decision tree lives in `ROUTER.md` Section 3. This reference covers the type table, disclosure stages and voice split that the tree feeds into.
28: 
29: ### When to Use
30: 
31: - Deciding which of the five README types a folder needs
32: - Setting how much a reader gets at each disclosure stage
33: - Splitting narrative and reference voice inside one file
34: 
35: ### Core Principle
36: 
37: Help users succeed in under 2 minutes, then provide depth for those who need it.
38: 
39: ---
40: 
41: ## 2. FIVE README TYPES
42: 
43: | Type | Location | Audience | Voice |
44: |------|----------|----------|-------|
45: | **Project** | `/README.md` | New contributors, evaluators | Two-tier (narrative + reference) |
46: | **Skill** | `.skilled/skills/[name]/README.md` | Humans understanding the skill | Two-tier (narrative + reference) |
47: | **Feature** | `/docs/features/[name]/README.md` | Developers implementing or maintaining | Two-tier (narrative + reference) |
48: | **Component** | `/src/components/[name]/README.md` | Developers using the component | Technical (reference only) |
49: | **Code Folder** | `[code-dir]/README.md` | Developers reading or modifying code | Technical (reference only) |
50: 
51: Project, Skill and Feature READMEs use both voice tiers. Component and Code Folder READMEs use the reference tier only.
52: 
53: ### Front-Page vs Technical Register
54: 
55: One Project README is also the repository's front page: `/README.md`. It may use the marketing register: value-first ordering and benefit-led headings, with decorative emoji on section headings, because its job is to win the reader's attention in seconds.
56: 
57: Every other README, including Skill and Feature, keeps the technical register for formatting:
58: 
59: - Numbered ALL-CAPS sections.
60: - Tables for lookups.
61: - Only semantic emoji (✅ ❌ ⚠️ 🔒 🚨) for rules and status markers.
62: 
63: The writing voice may still borrow the front page's engagement: a skill README may open with a pitch and benefit-led bullets before the technical detail. It explains rather than sells, and it never copies the decorative section emoji.
64: 
65: ---
66: 
67: ## 3. PROGRESSIVE DISCLOSURE
68: 
69: Essential information first, details on demand.
70: 
71: | Stage | Time | What the Reader Gets |
72: |-------|------|---------------------|
73: | Title + one-line tagline | 10 seconds | "What is this?" |
74: | Overview section | 30 seconds | "Should I care?" |
75: | Quick Start | 2 minutes | "How do I get it working?" |
76: | Full documentation | As needed | "How does everything work?" |
77: 
78: Title and tagline answer "what is this". Overview helps the reader decide relevance. Quick Start appears only when there is a runnable path. Detailed reference comes last.
79: 
80: ---
81: 
82: ## 4. TWO-TIER VOICE
83: 
84: Documents serving mixed audiences (newcomers through experts) use two writing voices in the same file.
85: 
86: **Narrative tier** explains what things do and why they matter. It uses analogies, plain language and active voice. It appears in section intros, Overview, Quick Start and the narrative half of Features (for example, "3.1 How It Works").
87: 
88: **Reference tier** carries precise parameter tables, configuration flags and tool signatures. It is terse and scannable. It appears in the reference half of Features (for example, "3.2 Tool Reference"), Configuration and Related Documents.
89: 
90: ### Worked Examples
91: 
92: **Narrative tier** (for Overview, Quick Start, Features 3.1):
93: 
94: > When you search for something, the system does not just look in one place. It checks several sources at once, like a librarian who checks the card catalog, the shelf labels and the reading room sign-out sheet all at the same time.
95: 
96: **Reference tier** (for Features 3.2, Configuration):
97: 
98: | Parameter | Type | Notes |
99: |-----------|------|-------|
100: | `query` | string | Free-text search query |
101: | `limit` | number | 1-100 results (default 10) |
102: 
103: ---
104: 
105: ## 5. CROSS-REFERENCES
106: 
107: - [writing-patterns.md](writing-patterns.md) - Per-section writing tips, analogy patterns and table patterns
108: - [quality-and-checklist.md](quality-and-checklist.md) - Quality criteria and pre-publish checklist
109: - [readme-template.md](../../assets/readme-template.md) - Fillable general README scaffold
110: - [hvr-rules.md](../../../sk-create-with-human-voice/references/hvr-rules.md) - Human Voice Rules

14: # AI Council Convergence Signals
15: 
16: This reference defines the lightweight v1 convergence signal and the conditions that prevent a council round from being called converged.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: Use `two-of-three-agree` for v1. If 2 of 3 seats endorse essentially the same plan and cross-critique produces no new high-severity findings, declare convergence and write `council-report.md`.
23: 
24: Agreement means the seats align on the material plan: implementation order, core risks, dependencies, and acceptance criteria. They do not need identical wording.
25: 
26: ---
27: 
28: ## 2. ESCAPE HATCHES
29: 
30: `max_rounds` reached without convergence: emit `council_complete` with `convergence:false`, preserve the competing plans, and recommend a user decision.
31: 
32: All seats fail in a round: do not fabricate convergence. Report the failed round with each seat status and ask for reframing or more context.
33: 
34: Single-seat endorsement: insufficient diversity. Re-run with stronger contrarian framing or a different vantage mix before calling the plan converged.
35: 
36: ---
37: 
38: ## 3. WHY SIMPLE FOR V1
39: 
40: ADR-001 keeps the convention lightweight. Sophisticated convergence math is non-goal N1 because the packet needs auditable output persistence, not a deep-skill state machine.
41: 
42: ---
43: 
44: ## 4. VALIDATOR GRADUATION
45: 
46: State schema and convergence fields are convention-only for v1. If drift appears in real council artifacts, graduate to a typed validator in a follow-on packet.
47: 
48: Cross-references:
49: - Agent body: `.skilled/agents/ai-council.md` §16
50: - Decision context: local doctor command ADRs ADR-001 and ADR-003
51: 
52: ---
53: 
54: ## Convergence Threshold Semantics
55: 
56: **Default:** 0.20 (proposed) on adjudicator-verdict stability across rounds
57: 
58: **Semantic:** the deep-ai-council threshold scores per-topic Round-N -> Round-N+1 verdict deltas from the adjudicator. Lower = more rounds / higher stability threshold.
59: 
60: **NOT INTERCHANGEABLE with siblings:**
61: - `deep-review` uses 0.10 default on weighted P0/P1/P2 severity ratio
62: - `deep-research` uses 0.05 default on newInfoRatio (negative-knowledge emphasis)
63: 
64: Carrying threshold expectations across siblings will cause unexpected iteration counts. See this skill's changelog and decision records for the cross-sibling threshold research and parity invariants that confirm thresholds do not carry across siblings.

30: `max_rounds` reached without convergence: emit `council_complete` with `convergence:false`, preserve the competing plans, and recommend a user decision.
31: 
32: All seats fail in a round: do not fabricate convergence. Report the failed round with each seat status and ask for reframing or more context.
33: 
34: Single-seat endorsement: insufficient diversity. Re-run with stronger contrarian framing or a different vantage mix before calling the plan converged.
35: 
36: ---
37: 
38: ## 3. WHY SIMPLE FOR V1
39: 
40: ADR-001 keeps the convention lightweight. Sophisticated convergence math is non-goal N1 because the packet needs auditable output persistence, not a deep-skill state machine.
41: 
42: ---
43: 
44: ## 4. VALIDATOR GRADUATION
45: 
46: State schema and convergence fields are convention-only for v1. If drift appears in real council artifacts, graduate to a typed validator in a follow-on packet.
47: 
48: Cross-references:
49: - Agent body: `.skilled/agents/ai-council.md` §16
50: - Decision context: local doctor command ADRs ADR-001 and ADR-003
51: 
52: ---
53: 
54: ## Convergence Threshold Semantics
55: 
56: **Default:** 0.20 (proposed) on adjudicator-verdict stability across rounds
57: 
58: **Semantic:** the deep-ai-council threshold scores per-topic Round-N -> Round-N+1 verdict deltas from the adjudicator. Lower = more rounds / higher stability threshold.
59: 
60: **NOT INTERCHANGEABLE with siblings:**
61: - `deep-review` uses 0.10 default on weighted P0/P1/P2 severity ratio
62: - `deep-research` uses 0.05 default on newInfoRatio (negative-knowledge emphasis)
63: 
64: Carrying threshold expectations across siblings will cause unexpected iteration counts. See this skill's changelog and decision records for the cross-sibling threshold research and parity invariants that confirm thresholds do not carry across siblings.

14: # Deep Mode Session Hierarchy
15: 
16: Deep mode organises council work as sessions containing topics which contain rounds. State files track progress and cost guards enforce limits.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. OVERVIEW
21: 
22: ### Core Principle
23: 
24: Session contains topics contain rounds. Each level has its own state file and guard checks.
25: 
26: ### When to Use
27: 
28: Use deep mode when you need multi-topic council sessions with cost controls and state persistence. Use shallow mode for single-topic quick decisions.
29: 
30: ### Key Sources
31: 
32: - Session orchestration: `scripts/orchestrate-session.cjs`
33: - Topic orchestration: `scripts/orchestrate-topic.cjs`
34: - Cost guards: `../../runtime//lib/council/cost-guards.cjs`
35: 
36: ---
37: 
38: ## 2. SESSION HIERARCHY
39: 
40: ### Session Level
41: 
42: A session is the top-level container. It holds multiple topics and enforces session-wide limits.
43: 
44: **Session state path**: `ai-council/session-state.jsonl`
45: 
46: **Session guard**: `max_topics_per_session` limits how many topics run
47: 
48: **Session saturation**: After `min_topics_before_session_saturation` topics, stability scores determine if the session should stop early
49: 
50: ### Topic Level
51: 
52: A topic is a single decision domain within a session. Topics run through rounds until stable or maxed out.
53: 
54: **Topic state path**: `ai-council/topics/{topic_id}/rounds/{round_id}/round-state.jsonl`
55: 
56: **Topic guard**: `max_rounds_per_topic` limits rounds per topic
57: 
58: **Cross-topic priors**: After the first topic, prior findings from other topics enrich the topic brief
59: 
60: ### Round Level
61: 
62: A round is one pass through the council seats. Seats dispatch, return verdicts and an adjudicator synthesises.
63: 
64: **Round state path**: Same as topic state path, one file per round
65: 
66: **Round guard**: `saturation_threshold` stops the topic when verdicts stop changing
67: 
68: ---
69: 
70: ## 3. STATE FILES
71: 
72: ### session-state.jsonl
73: 
74: Append-only JSONL at the session level. Records topic completion events.
75: 
76: **Event type**: `topic_completed`
77: 
78: **Payload includes**:
79: - `session_id`
80: - `topic_id`
81: - `topic_number`
82: - `rounds_completed`
83: - `final_verdict`
84: - `stability_score`
85: - `topic_stop_reason`
86: 
87: ### round-state.jsonl
88: 
89: Append-only JSONL at the round level. Records round progress events.
90: 
91: **Event type**: `round_completed`
92: 
93: **Payload includes**:
94: - `topic_id`
95: - `round_id`
96: - `round_number`
97: - `seats`
98: - `dispatch_summary`
99: - `adjudicator_verdict`
100: - `verdict_delta_from_previous`
101: - `verdict_stable`
102: - `stop_reason`
103: 
104: ---
105: 
106: ## 4. COST GUARDS
107: 
108: ### Guard Normalisation
109: 
110: Guards merge from session state and executor config. Executor config overrides session defaults
111: 
112: ### Guard Evaluation
113: 
114: `evaluateCouncilCostGuards` checks if limits are exceeded and returns stop reasons
115: 
116: **Stop reasons**:
117: - `max_topics_per_session`
118: - `saturation_threshold`
119: - `max_rounds_per_topic`
120: - `all_seats_failed`
121: 
122: ---
123: 
124: ## 5. DEEP-LOOP-RUNTIME DEPENDENCY
125: 
126: ### Required Modules
127: 
128: Deep mode imports council primitives from runtime/:
129: 
130: - `round-state-jsonl.cjs` for state file writes
131: - `cost-guards.cjs` for guard evaluation
132: - `session-state-hierarchy.cjs` for validation
133: - `multi-seat-dispatch.cjs` for seat execution
134: - `adjudicator-verdict-scoring.cjs` for stability scoring
135: 
136: ### Session State Validation
137: 
138: `validateSessionStateHierarchy` checks that session -> topic -> round structure is well-formed before orchestration starts
139: 
140: ---
141: 
142: ## 6. WORKED EXAMPLE
143: 
144: ### Session Flow
145: 
146: ```javascript
147: const result = await orchestrateSession({
148:   session_state: {
149:     session: {
150:       session_id: 'council-001',
151:       spec_folder: '/path/to/packet',
152:       max_topics_per_session: 5,
153:       max_rounds_per_topic: 3,
154:     },
155:     topics: [
156:       { topic_id: 'topic-001-runtime', title: 'Runtime Boundary' },
157:       { topic_id: 'topic-002-convergence', title: 'Convergence Semantics' },
158:     ],
159:     current: { round: { seats: ['seat-001', 'seat-002', 'seat-003'] } },
160:   },
161:   executor_config: {
162:     cost_guards: {
163:       max_topics_per_session: 5,
164:       saturation_threshold: 0.2,
165:       min_topics_before_session_saturation: 2,
166:     },
167:     orchestrateTopic: async ({ topic_id }) => {
168:       // Topic runner implementation
169:       return { topic_id, rounds_completed: 1, stability_score: 0.1 };
170:     },
171:   },
172: });
173: ```
174: 
175: **Result structure**:
176: - `session_id`
177: - `topics_completed`
178: - `topic_results`
179: - `skipped_topic_ids`
180: - `stop_reason`
181: - `session_state_path`
182:

14: # README Template and Selection Guide
15: 
16: Use this template for project, skill, feature and component READMEs. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) for source-folder READMEs that explain package topology, files, boundaries and data or control flow.
17: 
18: ---
19: 
20: ## 1. README SELECTION
21: 
22: README files answer two questions: what is this, and how does someone use or navigate it?
23: 
24: | Type | Use When | Template |
25: |---|---|---|
26: | Project | The repository or package needs a public entry point | This file |
27: | Skill | A skill needs human-facing context beyond `SKILL.md` | This file |
28: | Feature | A user-facing feature needs setup, usage or behavior notes | This file |
29: | Component | A reusable module has an API, examples or configuration | This file, trimmed |
30: | Code Folder | A source directory needs developer orientation | [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md) |
31: 
32: Create a README when someone can land in the folder and needs orientation. Skip it when inline comments or a nearby parent README already explain the folder.
33: 
34: ```text
35: Is this a project, package, skill or feature root?
36: +-- Yes: write a general README.
37: `-- No: is this source-code orientation?
38:     +-- Yes: use readme_code_template.md.
39:     `-- No: write a focused README only if readers need setup, usage or navigation help.
40: ```
41: 
42: Keep READMEs current-state only. Do not cite spec packet numbers, phase IDs or migration history. Use feature names, file paths, commands and stable source links.
43: 
44: ---
45: 
46: ## 2. GENERAL STRUCTURE
47: 
48: Use only the sections that fit the audience. Project and skill READMEs often need most sections. Feature and component READMEs should stay shorter.
49: 
50: | Section | Include When | Content |
51: |---|---|---|
52: | Overview | Always | Purpose, audience, main value and prerequisites |
53: | Key Statistics | Useful facts help readers decide scope | Counts, version, supported modes, limits |
54: | How This Compares | Readers may confuse this with nearby tools | Short comparison table |
55: | Quick Start | Readers need to run or try something | Short setup, verification and first use |
56: | Features | Capabilities need explanation | Feature groups, behavior notes and examples |
57: | Requirements | Runtime, tool or service needs exist | Minimum versions, permissions and external services |
58: | Structure | Navigation matters | Directory tree and key files |
59: | Configuration | Settings exist | Config files, options, defaults and env vars |
60: | Usage Examples | Patterns are easier shown than described | Simple and advanced examples with expected results |
61: | Troubleshooting | Users can hit known issues | What they see, cause and fix |
62: | FAQ | Repeated questions exist | Short answers only |
63: | Related Resources | Always when links exist | Grouped skills, documents, commands or external references |
64: 
65: Code-folder READMEs are different. Do not force Quick Start, Features, FAQ or Troubleshooting unless the directory has runnable commands or known reader problems. Use [`readme-code-template.md`](./readme-code-template.md).
66: 
67: ---
68: 
69: ## 3. SKILL AND PROJECT PROFILE
70: 
71: Use this profile for OpenCode skills, package roots and project-level READMEs that need more than a bare overview.
72: 
73: | Profile Block | Good For | Keep It Short By |
74: |---|---|---|
75: | `trigger_phrases` | Search, memory and skill routing | 3-8 concrete phrases |
76: | Key Statistics | Skill counts, tool counts, version facts | Use one compact table |
77: | How This Compares | Neighboring skills or tools | Compare only reader-relevant differences |
78: | Key Features | Current capability inventory | Group related features |
79: | Requirements | Tooling and runtime needs | Separate required from optional |
80: | Related Skills | Skill graph navigation | Group by relationship type |
81: | Related Documents | Operator or developer references | Link stable docs, not packet history |
82: | FAQ | Repeated questions | 3-6 high-value Q&A pairs |
83: 
84: Sections use plain numbered H2 headings. Do not add `<!-- ANCHOR -->` comments or a Table of Contents.
85: 
86: ```markdown
87: ## 1. OVERVIEW
88: 
89: [Section content]
90: 
91: ```
92: 
93: ---
94: 
95: ## 4. WRITING RULES
96: 
97: Write for scanning first.
98: 
99: - Lead with what the thing does.
100: - Put the fastest useful path before detailed reference.
101: - Use tables for options, file lists and comparisons.
102: - Give every inventory item a description. When an item needs more than one line, switch to the itemized pattern below instead of widening the table.
103: - Use fenced code blocks with language tags.
104: - Test commands before documenting them.
105: - Show expected output for verification commands.
106: - Use relative links for local docs.
107: - Remove unused sections instead of leaving placeholders.
108: 
109: The itemized pattern for inventories where each item needs more than one line:
110: 
111: ```markdown
112: **`spec.md`**
113: - What the feature is and why it exists.
114: - Required at every level.
115: ```
116: 
117: Group related items under an unnumbered `#####` heading when the inventory has natural groups, for example by how each item is triggered.
118: 
119: Voice by README type:
120: 
121: | Type | Voice |
122: |---|---|
123: | Project, Skill, Feature | Plain explanation first, reference detail later |
124: | Component | Technical and concise |

126: 
127: Human Voice Rules apply to all README content:
128: 
129: - No em dashes. Use commas, periods or colons.
130: - No semicolons. Split the sentence or use "and".
131: - No Oxford comma in inline lists.
132: - No setup phrases.
133: - No banned words from the HVR reference.
134: - Prefer active voice and direct verbs.

137:

140: ## 5. FRONTMATTER
141:

143:

145: ---
146: title: "[DOCUMENT_TITLE]"
147: description: "[One-sentence description]"
148: trigger_phrases:

150:   - "[routing phrase]"
151: ---
152: ```
